paragraphs: If the reader has understood what I have already said about literature in general, he will have no difficulty seeing what kind of influence a democratic social condition and democratic institutions can have on language itself, which is the chief instrument of thought.

American authors can truly be said to live more in England than in their own country, since they constantly study the English writers and take them as their models every day. But this is not true of the bulk of the population, which is more directly exposed to the particular causes at work in the United States. So it is not the written language but the spoken language that we must watch, if we want to detect the changes an aristocratic people’s idiom may undergo when it becomes the language of a democracy.

Educated Englishmen, who are better judges than I am of the finer shades of expression, have often assured me that the language of the educated classes in the United States is noticeably different from that of the educated classes in Great Britain. They complain not only that the Americans have brought a number of new words into use — the difference and the distance between the two countries might be enough to explain that much — but that these new words are drawn especially from the jargon of parties, the mechanical arts, or the language of trade. They also say that the Americans often use old English words in new senses. Finally, they say that the inhabitants of the United States frequently mix their phrasing in the strangest way, and sometimes put together words that are always kept apart in the language of the mother country. These remarks were made to me at various times by people who seemed to deserve credit, and they led me to reflect on the subject. My reflections brought me, by theoretical reasoning, to the same point that my informants had reached by practical observation.

In aristocracies, language naturally shares in the state of repose in which everything else stays. Few new words are coined, because few new things are made; and even if new things were made, they would be called by familiar words whose meaning has been fixed by tradition. If the human mind does at last stir itself, or is roused by light breaking in from outside, the new expressions it introduces carry a degree of learning, intelligence, and philosophy that shows they do not originate in a democracy. After the fall of Constantinople turned the tide of science and literature toward the west, the French language was almost immediately flooded with a multitude of new words, all with Greek or Latin roots. A learned neologism then sprang up in France. It stayed within the educated classes and had no noticeable effect on the people, or at most a very gradual one. All the nations of Europe showed the same change in turn. Milton alone introduced more than six hundred words into the English language, almost all of them derived from Latin, Greek, or Hebrew. In a democratic community, by contrast, the constant agitation tends unceasingly to change the character of the language, just as it changes the look of public affairs. In the midst of this general stir and rivalry of minds, a great number of new ideas are formed. Old ideas are lost, or reappear, or are divided into an infinite variety of minor shades. The result is that many words must fall out of use, and others must be brought in.

Democratic nations love change for its own sake, and this shows in their language as much as in their politics. Even when they have no need to change words, they sometimes feel a wish to transform them. The genius of a democratic people shows itself not only in the great number of words they bring into use, but also in the nature of the ideas those new words stand for. Among such a people the majority lays down the law in language as it does in everything else, and its prevailing spirit is as plain there as anywhere. But the majority is more occupied with business than with study, with political and commercial interests than with philosophical speculation or literary pursuits. Most of the words coined or adopted for its use will therefore bear the mark of these habits. They will mainly serve to express the needs of business, the passions of party, or the details of public administration. In these areas the language will keep spreading, while in metaphysics and theology it will gradually lose ground.

The source from which democratic nations usually draw their new expressions, and the way they go about coining them, are both easy to describe. People living in democratic countries know little of the language spoken at Athens and Rome, and they do not care to dig into the lore of antiquity to find the expression they happen to want. If they sometimes turn to learned etymologies, vanity will lead them to search the roots of the dead languages, but erudition does not naturally supply them with its resources. It sometimes happens that the most ignorant make the most use of them. The eminently democratic desire to rise above one’s own sphere will often lead them to dignify a common profession with a Greek or Latin name. The lower the calling and the further from learning, the more pompous and learned its name. Thus the French rope-dancers have transformed themselves into acrobates and funambules.

Lacking knowledge of the dead languages, democratic nations are inclined to borrow words from living tongues. Their dealings with one another become constant, and the inhabitants of different countries imitate each other more readily as they grow more alike every day.

But it is chiefly in their own languages that democratic nations attempt innovations. From time to time they take forgotten expressions out of their vocabulary and bring them back into use. Or they borrow from some particular class of the community a term peculiar to it and introduce it, with a figurative meaning, into the language of daily life. Many expressions that originally belonged to the technical language of a profession or a party are drawn in this way into general circulation.

The most common way democratic nations innovate in language is to give an unusual meaning to an expression already in use. This method is very simple, quick, and convenient. No learning is required to use it correctly, and ignorance itself rather helps the practice. But that practice is most dangerous to the language. When a democratic people doubles the meaning of a word in this way, they sometimes make the meaning it keeps as ambiguous as the one it gains. An author begins by slightly bending a known expression away from its original meaning, and he adapts it, thus modified, as well as he can to his subject. A second writer twists the sense of the expression in another direction; a third takes it over for another purpose. Since there is no common appeal to the judgment of a permanent tribunal that could settle the meaning of the word once and for all, it remains ambiguous. The consequence is that writers hardly ever seem to dwell on a single thought. They always seem to aim at a knot of ideas, leaving the reader to judge which of them has been hit. This is a deplorable consequence of democracy. I would rather have the language made hideous with words imported from the Chinese, the Tartars, or the Hurons than have the meaning of a word in our own language become indeterminate. Harmony and uniformity are only secondary beauties in composition. Many of these things are conventional, and strictly speaking it is possible to do without them. But without clear phrasing there is no good language.

The principle of equality necessarily introduces several other changes into language. In aristocratic ages, each nation tends to stand apart from all others and likes to have distinct characteristics of its own. It often happens, then, that several peoples with a common origin become estranged from one another, so that, without ceasing to understand the same language, they no longer all speak it in the same way. In these ages each nation is divided into a certain number of classes that see little of each other and do not mingle. Each of these classes acquires, and invariably keeps, habits of mind peculiar to itself, and chooses certain words and terms that afterward pass from generation to generation, like their estates. The same idiom then includes a language of the poor and a language of the rich, a language of the citizen and a language of the nobility, a learned language and a vulgar one. The deeper the divisions and the more impassable the barriers of society, the more this must be so. I would wager that among the castes of India there are amazing variations of language, and that there is almost as much difference between the language of the pariah and that of the Brahmin as there is in their dress. When, on the contrary, people are no longer restrained by ranks and meet on terms of constant contact — when castes are destroyed and the classes of society are recruited from one another and intermixed — all the words of a language are mingled. Those unsuitable to the greater number die out. The rest form a common store, from which everyone chooses pretty much at random. Almost all the different dialects that divided the idioms of the European nations are clearly declining. There is no patois in the New World, and it is disappearing every day from the old countries.

This revolution in social conditions affects style as much as it affects phrasing. Not only does everyone use the same words, but a habit grows up of using them without discrimination. The rules that style had set up are almost abolished. The line ceases to be drawn between expressions that seem vulgar by their very nature and others that seem refined. People who come from different ranks of society carry the terms and expressions they are used to into whatever circumstances they pass into. Thus the origin of words is lost, like the origin of individuals, and there is as much confusion in language as there is in society.

I am aware that in the classification of words there are rules that belong to no one form of society more than another, but come from the nature of things. Some expressions and phrases are vulgar because the ideas they are meant to express are low in themselves. Others are of a higher character because the objects they are meant to designate are naturally elevated. No mixing of ranks will ever erase these differences. But the principle of equality cannot fail to root out whatever is merely conventional and arbitrary in the forms of thought. Perhaps the necessary classification I pointed out in the last sentence will always be less respected by a democratic people than by any other. For among such a people there are no men permanently disposed, by education, culture, and leisure, to study the natural laws of language, and who make those laws respected by observing them themselves.

I will not leave this topic without touching on a feature of democratic languages that is perhaps more characteristic of them than any other. It has already been shown that democratic nations have a taste, and sometimes a passion, for general ideas, and that this arises from their particular merits and defects. This liking for general ideas shows itself in democratic languages through the continual use of generic terms or abstract expressions, and through the way they are used. This is the great merit and the great imperfection of these languages. Democratic nations are passionately fond of generic terms and abstract expressions, because these modes of speech enlarge thought and assist the operations of the mind by letting it include several objects in a small compass. A French democratic writer will be inclined to say capacites in the abstract for men of capacity, without specifying the objects to which their capacity is applied. He will talk about actualities to designate in one word the things passing before his eyes at that moment, and he will take in under the term eventualities whatever may happen in the universe from the moment he speaks. Democratic writers are perpetually coining words of this kind, in which they refine the already abstract terms of the language into still further abstraction. What is more, to make their mode of speech more concise, they personify the subject of these abstract terms and make it act like a real entity. Thus they would say in French, “La force des choses veut que les capacites gouvernent.”

I cannot illustrate what I mean better than by my own example. I have often used the word “equality” in an absolute sense. Indeed, I have personified equality in several places, saying that equality does such and such things, or refrains from doing others. It may be affirmed that the writers of the age of Louis XIV would not have used these expressions. They would never have thought of using the word “equality” without applying it to some particular object, and they would rather have given up the term altogether than agree to make a living person of it.

These abstract terms, which abound in democratic languages and are used on every occasion without being attached to any particular fact, enlarge and obscure the thoughts they are meant to convey. They make the mode of speech more concise and the idea in it less clear. But where language is concerned, democratic nations prefer obscurity to labor. In fact, I do not know whether this loose style has some secret charm for those who speak and write among these nations. The men who live there are frequently left to the efforts of their own individual minds, so they are almost always prey to doubt. And since their situation in life is forever changing, they are never held fast to any of their opinions by the secure tenure of their fortunes. People living in democratic countries are therefore inclined to have unsettled ideas, and they need loose expressions to convey them. They never know whether the idea they express today will suit the new position they may occupy tomorrow, so they naturally develop a liking for abstract terms. An abstract term is like a box with a false bottom: you may put in it whatever ideas you please, and take them out again without being noticed.

Among all nations, generic and abstract terms form the basis of language. I do not, therefore, pretend to banish these terms from democratic languages. I simply remark that in the ages of democracy people have a special tendency to multiply words of this kind. They tend to take them always by themselves in their most abstract sense, and to use them on all occasions, even when the nature of the discourse does not require them.
